forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: County Durham eligible for £32.471m grant covering 90% of schools-funding deficit to March 2026
news_drafts.lead:
County Durham is eligible for a £32.471m High Needs Stability Grant, covering 90% of the deficit built up on its dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools, to 31 March 2026. The Department for Education approved the council's plan for special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) on 2 October 2026, which made it eligible. The Cabinet's quarter two forecast paper of 18 November says the value is subject to final audited outturn and written confirmation from the department, with payment expected on 30 November 2026.

With the grant, the cumulative DSG deficit at 31 March 2027 is forecast at £35.111m, from £67.185m forecast at quarter one. The DSG reserve stood at a £36.080m deficit at the start of the year, and the accumulated deficit in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities, is £39.723m. The remaining deficit, and any in the current and next financial year, stay in the DSG reserve until the statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps such deficits off the main balance sheet, ends on 31 March 2028.

The quarter two forecast for the DSG centrally retained block is a net in-year overspend of £31.256m for 2026/27, against £16.742m in 2025/26 and £31.105m forecast at quarter one. The paper attributes it to additional demand for SEND and "cash-flat" high needs funding. The council set a high needs budget deficit of £30.278m for the year.

news_drafts.headline: Durham County Council confirmed £32.472m high needs grant as its schools deficit reached £36.06m
news_drafts.lead:
Durham County Council received confirmation on 2 October 2026 of £32.472m of High Needs Stability Grant for 2026/27, subject to the grant's conditions and delivery of its Local Area Reform Plan for special educational needs and disabilities. The council's dedicated schools grant (DSG) deficit, an overspend on the government grant that funds schools, rose from £16.0m in 2024/25 to £36.060m at 31 March 2026, its external auditor reports to the Audit Committee.

The council submitted the plan to the Department for Education on 19 June 2026. The auditor's report says the grant is intended to provide funding equal to 90% of the cumulative deficit at the end of 2025/26. The council's Annual Governance Statement put the cumulative deficit at circa £40m, with 90% of it about £36m and circa £4m left over. It gives the in-year deficit in high needs, the part of school funding for those children, as circa £17m for 2025/26. The council's risk report forecasts a high needs in-year deficit of £31.105m for 2026/27, and £70.828m cumulative by 31 March 2027 without mitigating intervention. An earmarked reserve of £11m is set aside for future high needs pressures. The council forecasts a cumulative deficit of circa £114.0m by 2028/29.

The auditor identified no significant weaknesses in the council's arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness. It made two other recommendations, on the forecast DSG deficit and on managing the savings needed to close medium-term budget gaps. The statutory override, the government rule that keeps these deficits off the council's main balance sheet, ends on 31 March 2028.

news_drafts.headline: County Durham expects £32.471m grant, cutting forecast schools deficit to £35.111m from £67.185m
news_drafts.lead:
County Durham Council expects to receive a £32.471m High Needs Stability Grant. Its Cabinet papers say this will reduce the forecast cumulative deficit on the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools, at 31 March 2027 to £35.111m. The quarter 1 forecast was £67.185m.

The Department for Education approved the council's SEND Local Area Reform Plan on 2 October 2026. SEND stands for special educational needs and disabilities. The approval makes the council eligible for a grant covering 90% of its DSG deficit to 31 March 2026. Payment is expected on 30 November 2026, subject to final audited outturn and written confirmation from the department. The DSG reserve stood at a deficit of £36.080m at the start of the year.

In the same report, the high needs block, the part of school funding for children with SEND, is forecast to show a net in-year overspend of £31.256m for 2026/27, against £16.742m in 2025/26. The paper says the figure is slightly higher than at quarter 1 and reflects rising SEND demand and cash-flat high needs funding. The block's budget was set with a planned deficit of £30.278m. Forecast high needs spend for the year is £139.282m.

findings.committee: Corporate Overview and Scrutiny Management Board
findings.paper_title: item 6 Cabinet 18.11.26 - QTR2 Forecast of Outturn 2026-27 Final v2 (002)
findings.headline: Benfieldside Primary's licensed deficit will transfer to the Stanley Learning Partnership Multi-Academy Trust after its conversion on 1 September 2026
findings.detail: The school had a licensed revenue deficit for 2026/27 because it could not balance its budget with the resources available. The final balance on conversion will be reported on 31 December 2026, and any deficit will transfer to the Trust at that point.
findings.matters: A school deficit moving from a council to a multi-academy trust is a specific transfer of liability that other councils with converting schools will want to track.
findings.figures: One school converted from 1 September 2026; final balance to be reported 31 December 2026
findings.quote: any deficit will transfer to the Trust at that point

findings.committee: Corporate Overview and Scrutiny Management Board
findings.paper_title: item 6 Cabinet 18.11.26 - QTR2 Forecast of Outturn 2026-27 Final v2 (002)
findings.headline: Education and Skills forecasts a £0.785 million overspend after UK Shared Prosperity Funding for Progression and Learning is withdrawn
findings.detail: The paper says NEMSA has stated no further or additional funding will be provided for this service. The council will need to restructure and reduce 20 to 30 FTE posts to set a balanced budget for 2027/28 and beyond.
findings.matters: A council losing external funding for a service and having to cut posts to rebalance a budget is a clear example of how regional funding changes flow through to staffing.
findings.figures: £0.785 million forecast overspend; £0.217 million reserves used; 20 to 30 FTE posts to reduce; circa £1 million overspend if fully staffed
findings.quote: This will necessitate a reduction of 20 to 30 FTE posts in this service areas.

findings.committee: Corporate Overview and Scrutiny Management Board
findings.paper_title: item 6 Cabinet 18.11.26 - QTR2 Forecast of Outturn 2026-27 Final v2 (002)
findings.headline: Interest and investment income is forecast at £2.914 million above a £2.381 million base budget, because cash balances are higher than planned
findings.detail: The paper says the higher income comes from more cash being available because of slippage in capital spending, and from higher interest on external investments. It also says markets now expect possible interest rate rises late in 2026/27, where the budget had assumed rates would fall.
findings.matters: Investment income is offsetting a borrowing cost increase, and the council's position on it depends on capital slippage that will reverse as spending catches up.
findings.figures: £2.914 million overachievement; £2.381 million base budget assumption; £2.854 million quarter one overachievement; bank base rate 3.75%
findings.quote: The interest and investment income / dividends quarter two forecast shows an overachievement of £2.914 million against a base budget assumption of £2.381 million.

findings.committee: Corporate Overview and Scrutiny Management Board
findings.paper_title: item 6 Cabinet 18.11.26 - QTR2 Forecast of Outturn 2026-27 Final v2 (002)
findings.headline: Maintained schools forecast a net use of £0.316 million of reserves in 2026/27, against £4.027 million budgeted
findings.detail: The paper says 57 schools are forecasting an underspend that adds £4.222 million to reserves, and 65 schools are forecasting an overspend that draws £4.538 million. It attributes the improvement mainly to additional DSG income, including banding adjustments and SEN top-up funding.
findings.matters: School reserve drawdown is a leading indicator of which schools may move into deficit and the council's exposure to them.
findings.figures: £0.316 million net use of reserves; £4.027 million budgeted use; £3.711 million improvement; £4.222 million added by 57 schools; £4.538 million drawn by 65 schools; 123 maintained schools
findings.quote: The updated forecasts at quarter two show that schools will need to use a net £0.316 million of reserves to balance their in-year financial position

findings.committee: Corporate Overview and Scrutiny Management Board
findings.paper_title: item 6 Cabinet 18.11.26 - QTR2 Forecast of Outturn 2026-27 Final v2 (002)
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves excluding schools are forecast to fall by £20.975 million in 2026/27, from £183.857 million to £162.882 million
findings.detail: The quarter one forecast assumed a reduction of £19.499 million, so quarter two adds a further £1.476 million drawdown. The paper lists the largest movements as Extended Producer Responsibility and food waste grant reserves, the Corporate ER/VR reserve, and the Children Families and Youth Grant reserve.
findings.matters: A reserves fall of over £20 million in one year is a measure of how much one-off funding the council is spending on recurring pressures, which a peer or lender would compare against their own position.
findings.figures: £20.975 million forecast reduction; £183.857 million at 1 April 2026; £162.882 million at 31 March 2027; £19.499 million quarter one assumed reduction; £1.476 million additional drawdown; £1.922 million net EPR reserve drawdown
findings.quote: Total earmarked reserves (excluding schools reserves and the General Reserve) are now forecast to decrease by £20.975 million during 2026/27 from £183.857 million at 1 April 2026 to £162.882 million at 31 March 2027.

daily_post.headline: Maintained schools forecast a net use of £0.316 million of reserves in 2026/27, £3.711 million less than budgeted
daily_post.lead: A wide gap between budgeted and forecast school reserve use shows how school budgets are moving in-year, which finance officers at other councils would compare with their own schools' positions.
